title: The place
subtitle: The garden of France
objectives: Explain how climate changes along the river

steps.title: A long river
steps.body: The Loire is France's longest river, about 1,000 km. Vineyards line it for over 400 km, from the Atlantic near Nantes inland to Sancerre and Pouilly. The region is divided into four parts: the Pays Nantais, Anjou-Saumur, Touraine and the Central Vineyards. It's known as the garden of France.

steps.title: From maritime to continental
steps.body: Near the Atlantic, the Pays Nantais is maritime: mild and damp. Inland, through Anjou and Touraine, the climate becomes gradually more continental: warmer summers, colder winters. The Central Vineyards, near the centre of France, are continental. Throughout, the Loire is cool, keeping acidity high and alcohol moderate.

steps.prompt: How does the climate change as you move up the Loire from the Atlantic?

steps.title: Châteaux and kings
steps.body: The Loire was the playground of French kings in the Renaissance, who built châteaux like Chambord and Chenonceau. Many were built from tuffeau, a soft, white limestone. The caves dug to extract it now serve as cellars, especially in Saumur and Vouvray. The valley between Sully-sur-Loire and Chalonnes is a UNESCO site.

steps.prompt: Which are parts of the Loire wine region?

steps.title: What you learned
points: The Loire has four parts along 400 km of river
The climate shifts from maritime to continental
Tuffeau built its châteaux and cellars
